# The React client

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

`@expo/snapback-react` supplies a prepared provider, exact generated-reference
inference, shared single and grouped live queries, optimistic mutations,
managed presence, and connection state through React's `useSyncExternalStore`
contract. The provider owns canonical query and room identity, Strict Mode
replay, late-handle disposal, auth custody blanking, expiry/heartbeat work, and
cleanup. Components do not open live handles in `useEffect`, add a second
query cache, or manage presence intervals.

Prepare the connected deployment before rendering, then construct a provider
from that immutable binding:

```ts fragment reason="application composition varies by renderer and generated artifact imports"
const binding = await client.prepareReactBinding({
  generatedManifest: { schema, functions, capabilityManifest },
});
const provider = createSnapbackReactProvider(binding);

root.render(
  <SnapbackProvider provider={provider}>
    <App />
  </SnapbackProvider>,
);
```

Preparation verifies app, deployment, auth-mode, schema, function-catalog,
result contracts, ephemeral declarations, and capability identity. The
provider borrows the client; `provider.dispose()` drains provider-owned
subscriptions, rooms, stores, listeners, timers, connection grant, socket
demand, and its auth-barrier participant.

## Bind a generated query

Pass a generated operation reference and its exact arguments. The reference
supplies both argument and result types, so there is no result generic to fill
in or override:

```ts source=packages/snapback-react/exact-result-types.fixture.ts
const query = useSnapbackQuery(todos, { owner: 'ada' });
if (query.status === 'ready' || query.status === 'refreshing') {
  query.data[0]?.title.toUpperCase();
}
```

`useSnapbackQuery` returns:

- `status`: `pending | ready | refreshing | error | skipped`;
- `data`: immutable result rows only for `ready` or `refreshing`, otherwise
  `undefined`;
- `connection`: `idle | connecting | live | polling | stale | disconnected |
  closed | error`;
- `error`: a structured diagnostic for `error`, otherwise `null`;
- `freshness`: `unknown | retained | current` — `retained` rows came from
  the persisted cache (an offline cold boot) and are never presented as
  settled: a retained frame keeps `status: 'refreshing'` even on a live
  connection until the authoritative answer makes it `current`;
- `retention`: the headless handle's refuse-with-clarity retainability fact
  (`{ retainable, code, reason, store }`, `null` until classified) — see
  [offline retention](../sync/offline-and-retention.md) for the opt-in that
  makes a query retainable.

Same-reference, same-argument siblings under one provider share one store and
one upstream subscription while retaining independent React consumers.
Different provider objects, complete generated references, or canonical
arguments stay isolated.

## Read a query group

When the group is also a declared route bundle, use its generated reference.
Prepare it before mount so the LLP 0090 register-mode owner takes every
initial snapshot and creates every live registration at one commit:

```ts fragment reason="route and parameter names come from the generated application API"
const workspaceGroup = await binding.prepareQueryGroup(
  groups['/workspace/:incidentId'],
  { incidentId },
  { fallbackToLive: true },
);
const provider = createSnapbackReactProvider(binding, {
  preparedGroup: workspaceGroup,
});

// Inside the provider:
const workspace = useSnapbackQueries(workspaceGroup);
```

The generated reference closes the child refs, argument mappings, string route
parameters, app, and definition digest. The prepared group is opaque: its
`$param` mappings target string args only; numeric/boolean parameter routes
remain available through ordinary read bundles but do not receive a registered
group reference. Literal numeric/boolean args are fine. The prepared group's
public entries contain safe generated identity, never rows, subscription ids,
resume receipts, authorization projections, namespaces, grants, or a
connection handle, and the private transferred owner is not reachable through
provider properties. The provider publishes registered rows only after
positive server-confirmed socket attach. On a successful registered boot,
`workspace.boot` records the one initial
`{commitVersion, generation, versionStream, attachDeadline}` and each canonical
child store adopts its registration without an ordinary prime/subscribe race.
That field is initial provenance only; later child deltas are independently
live.

Fallback is intentionally narrow. Only a target whose served capability
manifest lacks experimental `registered_bundle_boot_v1` can produce
`source: "live-fallback"` when the author set `fallbackToLive: true`.
Authentication, authorization, integrity, limit, timeout, and malformed
bundle failures still refuse. If a valid registered preparation reaches its
attach deadline before provider adoption, the provider reports
`source: "live-recovery"`, `reason: "attach-deadline-expired"`, and
`boot: null`; it discards the expired rows and opens ordinary fresh live
subscriptions.

A lazy child is also fail-closed: if its registered subscription receives a
delta before that child store adopts it, the provider reports
`source: "live-recovery"`, `reason: "unadopted-delta"`, and `boot: null`.
First demand opens a fresh subscription that supersedes the dirty registration
instead of exposing the older bundle rows.

For view-local group membership that is not a route bundle, pass the existing
typed object map directly:

```ts fragment reason="view-local group membership is application-specific"
const filters = useSnapbackQueries({
  incidents: { ref: api.listIncidents, args: {} },
  tasks: { ref: api.tasksForIncident, args: { incidentId } },
  comments: { ref: api.commentsForIncident, args: showComments ? {} : skip },
});
```

Groups contain 1–64 entries. Each non-skipped child counts as one consumer and
one live subscription unless it shares an existing canonical store. Changing
one entry preserves unrelated entry snapshots. Validation and cap admission
are transactional: a refused update leaves the previous group attached.

## Run a mutation

```ts fragment reason="mutation names and fields come from the application schema"
const addTask = useSnapbackMutation(api.addTask);
const taskId = await addTask({ incidentId, body: 'Check headers' });
```

The returned function infers exact arguments and the unwrapped result from the
generated mutation reference. Runtime refusals reject with Snapback's
structured diagnostic.

For a mutation whose optimistic projection updates a currently authoritative
live query, declare that projection beside the hook:

```ts fragment reason="mutation and query fields come from the generated application API"
const toggleTask = useSnapbackMutation(api.toggleTask, {
  optimistic: {
    query: api.allTasks,
    args: {},
    update(tasks, { taskId }) {
      return tasks.map((task) =>
        task.id === taskId ? { ...task, done: !task.done } : task);
    },
    isAuthoritative(tasks, result) {
      return tasks.some((task) => task.id === result.id
        && task.done === result.done);
    },
  },
});
```

The optimistic layer is installed only over the provider's already-current
authoritative query store and is validated against the generated result
contract before network work. Overlapping attempts rebase in invocation order.
Rejection removes only its own layer and recomputes over the newest
authoritative base. An HTTP response validates and settles the mutation
promise, but is not itself live-query authority; `isAuthoritative`, when
present, retires that layer only after a matching validated live delivery.
There are at most 256 pending optimistic layers per store.

## Publish and observe presence

Pass a generated connection-keyed ephemeral reference. A non-skipped value is
declarative managed intent: the provider publishes it after the authoritative
room snapshot and refreshes it within the generated TTL and rate limits.

```ts fragment reason="presence fields come from the generated ephemeral declaration"
const presence = useSnapbackPresence(ephemeral.incidentPresence, {
  scope: { incidentId },
  value: {
    userId: persona.id,
    name: persona.name,
    color: persona.color,
    viewing: 'incident',
  },
  ttlMs: 4_000,
});

if (presence.status === 'ready' || presence.status === 'stale') {
  renderViewers(presence.entries);
}
```

Equal provider/reference/scope consumers share one headless room, overlay,
listener, and heartbeat. Their managed values and TTLs must agree. Use
`value: skip` for an observer; only observers may call `publish` and `delete`
imperatively. Managed TTL is 500 ms through the collection's generated
maximum, and scope/value contracts, payload size, sustained rate, burst rate,
and React-local room/consumer/publisher caps refuse before invalid work.

The closed state is `pending | resyncing | ready | stale | error |
unsupported`. Only `ready` is authoritative. `stale` retains same-authority
entries only to their server-stamped monotonic expiry; predecessor authority
entries are blanked. Presence is never persisted, hydrated, or counted as a
durable mutation. This first-class surface is deliberately local-target only;
a hosted binding returns `unsupported` without starting a room or socket.

## Render connection state honestly

`useSnapbackConnection()` observes the provider-wide weakest connection state
and active-subscription count without creating demand. Render `connecting`,
`live`, `polling`, `stale`, and `disconnected` as distinct facts. Retained data
under `refreshing` is useful but is not proof that the transport is currently
live.

The provider admits at most 256 cached query stores, 1,024 committed query
consumers, and 64 simultaneous server subscriptions. A saturated replacement
can supersede exactly one predecessor only when the updating group uniquely
owns it; shared or multi-entry saturated replacement refuses without changing
the old group.

This is an Online projection. It does not claim local handler execution or
Parity merely because it can retain data while a connection is stale.

## Render offline facts honestly

The hooks project the headless client's own offline facts — they surface,
never invent. An offline cold boot of a retainable query renders its
persisted rows with `freshness: 'retained'` and `status: 'refreshing'`
(never `'ready'`), holding the `stale` connection axis, and settles to
`freshness: 'current'` when the authoritative answer arrives:

```js source=packages/snapback-react/offline.test.mjs
  await act(async () => {
    handle.seedRetained(RETAINED_ROWS);
    handle.surviveOffline();
    await flush();
  });
  assert.equal(latest.freshness, 'retained');
  assert.equal(latest.status, 'refreshing');
  assert.equal(latest.connection, 'stale');
  assert.equal(latest.retention?.retainable, true);
```

`useSnapbackOutbox()` projects the durable queued-intent state
(LLP 0043 M2): `{ status, supported, pending, failed, replaying }` plus a
`replay()` action that drains through the client's single-flight
`replayQueuedMutations()`. Render a queued-changes badge from it next to
retained rows — the retained rows themselves stay **pre-intent** (this arm
runs no local execution, so queued writes are never fabricated into the
frame; LLP 0090 D3's rendering note). A client without the projection seam
refuses with `SNAPBACK_REACT_OUTBOX_UNSUPPORTED` instead of reporting a
false empty queue. `observeSnapbackOutbox(provider, listener)` is the
framework-neutral twin for acceptance adapters.

An optimistic mutation projection still requires a **current authoritative**
store: installing an optimistic layer over a retained-only frame refuses
with `SNAPBACK_REACT_OPTIMISTIC_STORE_MISSING`.

The retained Signal Desk receipt at
`demos/signal-desk/acceptance/results/react-presence.v1.json` proves two
independent WebSocket clients, TTL expiry, disconnect deletion, durable-version
separation, optimistic rebase/matcher ordering, SSR zero demand, hosted
no-work refusal, and exact provider/client/server cleanup with zero skips.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not construct a provider from an unprepared client.** Await
  `prepareReactBinding` before rendering.
- **Do not rebuild live ownership with `useEffect` and `useState`.** That
  reintroduces Strict Mode, sibling-sharing, and teardown races.
- **Do not key by `JSON.stringify(args)` in component code.** Pass args and
  generated references to the hook; the canonical identity contract owns them.
- **Do not add a parallel React query cache.** The external store is the shared
  current-value-plus-subscription seam.
- **Do not call Online local-first or Parity.** Those classes require the
  retained execution/replay proofs in LLP 0012 and LLP 0064.
- **Do not pass string names from components.** Pass generated query and
  mutation references admitted by the prepared binding.
- **Do not add a caller-selected row/result generic around a generated
  reference.** Fix the function's result contract and regenerate the API.
- **Do not treat a mutation HTTP response as live-query authority.** Use the
  subsequent validated live delivery to retire optimistic state.
- **Do not create presence heartbeat intervals in application code.** Pass
  managed intent to `useSnapbackPresence`; the provider owns admission,
  refresh, disconnect, and teardown.

# Swift client

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

`clients/swift/SnapbackClient` is the first non-JavaScript proving client. It
ships as a SwiftPM library for macOS 13+ and iOS 16+ and claims `poll/local`
and `live/local`. It does not yet claim `live/hosted`, offline `Parity`, or
sender-constrained native custody.

## Construct a client

Create `SnapbackClient.Configuration(baseURL:)`. For sessions mode, set
`sessionBearer` to a genuine Snapback session obtained through email-code auth
or the [supported external identity-broker seam](../auth/native-apps.md).
The client then:

- carries the bearer only in `Authorization`;
- offers `auth/rr` and `auth/live` at every exact boundary;
- omits caller-selected `userId` body auth;
- creates a stable authorization namespace per live query; and
- retries only HTTP 409 `SNAPBACK_AUTH_RESERVATION_STALE`, with a configurable
  40-attempt short-jitter budget.

Never package the server's admin token or impersonation capability in the app.

## Subscribe and receive every row lane

Call `openConnection()`, then `subscribe(function:args:)`. Start either
`startDrainLoop()` or `openLiveStream()`. `onUpdate` receives ordinary
replace/delta rows and authorization-invalidation snapshots through the same
callback.

Ordinary replace/delta lanes use a strict increasing data-version guard.
Authorization invalidation has its own exact scope/revision/ticket fence: a
first-seen satisfying snapshot can replace rows at the same data version, and
only an identical already-applied ticket is acknowledged again without
reapplying. Missing snapshot resolutions quarantine and blank the old
materialization. A `terminalDelete` resolution destroys rows, persists the
terminal fence, publishes the blank state, and ACKs without resubscribing.

## Bind app lifecycle

Call `pauseForBackground()` from the app's background/inactive transition. It
releases subscription demand, stops polling and heartbeat work, and closes the
socket while retaining the desired query specifications. Call
`resumeAfterForeground()` after the app becomes active; it reattaches the lane
and obtains fresh snapshots before resuming live publication.

If the server reports `SNAPBACK_CONNECTION_TOKEN_INVALID` after idle reaping
or grant expiry, the client discards that grant and quiesces its transports.
The next foreground attempt opens a fresh grant and re-establishes every
desired subscription; it never loops on the refused token.

These are platform-neutral methods. A SwiftUI host can map `scenePhase` to
them; UIKit can map the corresponding application notifications. Do not put
reconnect logic in individual views.

## Verify changes

From `clients/swift/SnapbackClient`, run `swift test`. The suite replays the
committed conformance corpus and adds client-specific coverage for invalidation
apply-before-ack (including equal data versions), terminal deletion, exact
duplicate redelivery, foreground grant-loss recovery, body-auth omission, and
reservation retry exhaustion/eventual success.

## Support status

Swift is the maintained proving client in this repository. Kotlin and Dart
implementations produced during the Partitime clean-room run are reference
evidence, not committed or published first-party artifacts. Do not tell users
to depend on them until their packaging, ownership, and CI gates land; the
[capability index](../capabilities.md) keeps that gap explicit.

## Anti-patterns

- Do not embed admin or impersonation secrets in a native bundle.
- Do not set `userId` in sessions-mode bodies.
- Do not reconnect without fresh subscription snapshots.
- Do not ACK an unapplied authorization snapshot.
- Do not claim hosted or sender-constrained native auth from local bearer
  evidence.

# React Expo Online clients

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

React Native/Expo uses the same `@expo/snapback-client`, generated function
references, framework-neutral external store, and `@expo/snapback-react` hook as
React web. It is an **Online** surface: queries and mutations run against a
reachable Snapback backend. It does not execute handlers locally and therefore
does not claim local-first behavior or Parity.

The current implementation has independent clean seven-check Android emulator
and iOS Simulator receipts. Each binds its implementation revision, hashed
carrier/build inputs, release build and artifact digest, so both
`STEP2.REACT_EXPO_ANDROID_ONLINE` and `STEP2.REACT_EXPO_IOS_ONLINE` are passing.
Treat this page as the shipped API plus the exact current evidence boundary,
not as a physical-device or production-support declaration.

## Use the same generated API and hook

The carrier imports project-generated refs and binds them through the ordinary
React hook:

```tsx source=demos/competitive-checkpoint/surfaces/react-expo/App.tsx
  const conversations = useSnapbackQuery<Conversation>({
    provider: checkpointProvider,
    query: api.listConversations,
    userId: USER_ID,
    authority: USER_ID,
  });
```

The package compatibility layer resolves that immutable reference for the
provider; application code never supplies a string function name. There is no
direct table-write API or second native cache. The provider declares the exact
`snapback.external-store.v1` compatibility token. A different token refuses
before application data is published.

## Prove one operating-system tuple at a time

Run the profile gate with an explicit OS and receipt:

```sh
node demos/partiful-matrix/tests/acceptance/native-react-expo.mjs \
  --platform ios \
  --receipt demos/partiful-matrix/acceptance/results/step2-react-expo-ios.json
```

The OS-specific receipt must prove all seven LLP 0064 facts:

1. release carrier build and emulator/device launch;
2. generated-function initial authoritative data;
3. optimistic pending followed by authoritative settlement;
4. authority rotation followed by a fresh query;
5. background and foreground lifecycle events;
6. retained prior rows while offline, then authoritative reconnect; and
7. release-artifact exclusion of Snapback server code.

Android acceptance uses `adb reverse`; iOS acceptance launches the release app
in the selected simulator and backgrounds it by launching Settings through
`simctl`. Both bridge to a loopback development server and witness collector.
That is test infrastructure, not a production endpoint design and not
permission to expose development auth on a non-loopback listener. Each OS must
run its own build, lifecycle, reconnect, and artifact-exclusion checks; neither
receipt can substitute for the other.

## Handle native reconnect honestly

React Native WebSockets may emit `error` without the browser-style follow-up
`close`. The shared stream manager treats that error as connection loss,
refreshes the connection grant, and re-enters through a fresh
snapshot-with-subscribe. During the gap, keep the prior rows visible under a
`stale` or disconnected connection fact; never relabel them live.

Backgrounding quiesces the provider's live handles while retaining rendered
rows; foregrounding restarts the surviving current-authority subscriptions and
waits for authoritative snapshots. The Online gate asserts those provider
transitions in addition to the OS events. It does not claim the durable queue,
local execution, replay/rebase, or authority-safe retained store required for
Exact Native Parity.

Use `bindSnapbackAppLifecycle(AppState, liveHandle)` from `@expo/snapback-react`
(or `@expo/snapback-client/online`) when a provider exposes the first-party
`liveQuery` handle. The helper has no React Native package dependency: it
serializes AppState changes onto the handle's `pause()` / `resume()` methods
and removes the listener on disposal. This is the supported replacement for a
timer that tears down a merely quiet socket.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not transfer evidence between operating systems.** Native evidence is
  per immutable surface/OS profile.
- **Do not call Online local-first or Parity.** No local handler execution is
  claimed.
- **Do not bundle the Snapback server into the carrier.** Native packages
  contain public generated client artifacts only.
- **Do not replace generated function refs with stringly table calls.** The
  generated API is the cross-surface contract.
- **Do not ship emulator port bridging as endpoint security.** It is local
  acceptance infrastructure only.

# Framework bindings

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A query hook is the small part. React and Contract bindings ship today; no
first-party Vue, Svelte, or Solid package is claimed. Those systems can
adapt “current rows plus subscribe” in well under 100 lines. A valuable
Snapback binding centralizes the lifecycle and failure behavior that otherwise
fails silently.

## Build on the external store

Use `snapback.external-store.v1` from `@expo/snapback-client/external-store`.
It owns canonical query identity, same-key sibling sharing, late-handle
resolution, stale-generation fencing, error/connection snapshots, optimistic
settlement, refcounts, and final disposal. Project that store into the
framework's native subscription primitive.

Do not add a second query cache, socket owner, or mutation settlement model.

## Own the hard transitions

A binding must cover:

| Transition | Required behavior |
| --- | --- |
| identity changes | retire predecessor scope, synchronously blank protected rows, subscribe under successor authority |
| socket loss | surface stale/connecting state, obtain a fresh grant when needed, fresh subscribe with supersession |
| background | call the provider handle's `pause()`; release demand and quiesce retries |
| foreground | call `resume()`; reconcile authority, reconnect, and fresh-subscribe |
| invalidation | publish the atomic replacement only after version guard; ACK after apply |
| transient reservation conflict | retry only the exact typed refusal within the client budget |
| terminal auth | expose an error state and blank predecessor materialization before callbacks resume |
| scope disposal | release every handle even if an observer throws |

High-level handle disposal is idempotent after its own logout or terminal
authority retirement. Keep that exact-handle behavior in the binding; do not
catch arbitrary low-level `unsubscribeLive` errors, because foreign ids and
ownership/session mismatches remain fail-closed. View unmount may ignore the
returned cleanup task after synchronous local teardown; lifecycle tests and
operational cleanup should await it so genuine typed failures stay visible.

The headless JS handle already supplies `pause()`, `resume()`, `dispose()`,
connection events, and error state. Native clients expose equivalent
provider-level lifecycle hooks. Bind host lifecycle once at the provider
boundary, not in every component.

## Keep errors as state

A rejected setup promise is not enough: after initial render, reconnect,
authorization, and server diagnostics are ongoing state. The framework
projection should expose rows, connection phase, and the latest structured
error together. Preserve the diagnostic code; do not reduce it to a boolean.

## Test the binding, not its syntax

The acceptance suite should prove identity rotation, background/foreground,
socket-loss re-grant, version regression refusal, typed retry, observer-throw
cleanup, and final unmount disposal. A hook unit test that only receives one
row update does not establish a useful binding.

## Anti-patterns

- Do not publish a framework package whose only value is a query hook.
- Do not let view mount/unmount own server demand directly.
- Do not preserve predecessor rows across an authority change.
- Do not swallow structured diagnostics into console logging.
- Do not reconnect a socket without re-establishing its subscriptions.

---

# Build an immutable release

`snapback deploy build` closes and retains the target-neutral input to a
deployment adapter. It does not upload, provision, activate, or claim a hosted
application. The resulting manifest is deliberately activation-ineligible and
lists every missing hosted or supply-chain proof as a blocking GAP.

## Build and verify the release closure

Run generation and release construction from the application root:

```sh
snapback deploy build snapback \
  --target-profile local-dev-sqlite-ibex \
  --web-dist dist-web \
  --json
```

The default store is `.snapback/releases/<release digest>/`. Pass `--output`
to retain the closure elsewhere. A successful result has
`schemaVersion: snapback.deploy-build.v1` and reports the release id, manifest
digest, component count, byte count, source posture, and blocking GAPs.

The command regenerates the app, verifies that its schema, function, and
capability manifests agree with the selected target profile, and collects the
generated artifacts, package manifest, dependency lock, and optional web
distribution. It then:

- rejects symlinks, path overlap/escape, source maps, local databases, dotenv
  files, npm credentials, private keys, and known credential patterns;
- enforces the v1 file and byte budgets;
- records the Git revision, commit timestamp, tool versions, dirty-state fact,
  compatibility digests, capabilities, scans, and every component digest;
- derives `releaseId` from canonical manifest content;
- copies through a private staging directory and verifies every copied byte;
  and
- reopens the completed closure and refuses undeclared, missing, or changed
  files.

Building the same clean inputs reuses the same verified release. The output
store is excluded from the source-dirty calculation, so a retained default
release does not poison the next build.

## Handle dirty preview input explicitly

A dirty tree fails with `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_DIRTY_SOURCE`. For a non-production
preview only, opt in:

```sh
snapback deploy build snapback --allow-dirty --json
```

The manifest retains `source.dirty: true` and a digest of the dirty path facts
without disclosing the path list. Dirty input never becomes activation
eligible in this target-neutral command.

## Read GAPs before choosing an adapter

Every v1 release has `activationEligible: false`. It names missing adapter,
runtime, signing, provenance, SBOM, migration, probe, logs, inspection,
rollback, backup/restore, and TLS evidence, plus target capability gaps. A
future adapter may add artifacts and receipts only under the LLP 0072
identity/plan/apply contract; it may not reinterpret this result as deployment
success.

The existing [Cloudflare proof](./cloudflare.md) remains a separate, narrow
repository workflow. It is not wired to `snapback deploy build`, and neither
surface currently satisfies the complete hosted profile.

## Register one exact container/VM target

Create a descriptor conforming to
`schemas/target.descriptor.schema.json`, then register it outside the source
tree:

```sh
snapback target add \
  --descriptor ~/.config/snapback/preview-target.json \
  --control-root ~/.local/state/snapback/control \
  --json
```

The descriptor binds the project, target, environment, deployment, database,
stream incarnation, target profile, production class, provider account, region,
HTTPS origin, and `singleInstanceContainerVm` adapter version. `driverPath` is
absolute and `driverSha256` pins the executable bytes. `credentialRef` names an
OS or provider secret-store handle; a credential value is not a valid field.
Credential and state references reject URI userinfo, query, and fragment
components so an apparently opaque handle cannot smuggle inline authority.

The control root, target registry, and retained plans must be owner-only.
Registration is idempotent for identical canonical bytes and refuses to reuse a
`targetId` for any different descriptor. Every later read rechecks the adapter
digest, so replacing the executable invalidates the registration rather than
silently changing its authority.

Inspect the registration and require fresh provider read-back:

```sh
snapback target show target-preview-1 --json
snapback target doctor target-preview-1 --json
snapback deploy status --target target-preview-1 --json
```

The adapter receives one closed JSON request on stdin with no argv arguments and
an allowlisted environment. Snapback rejects a different provider account,
region, origin, deployment, database, stream, or target profile even when the
adapter exits successfully.

## Pin the remote drill before provisioning

An adapter integration calls `createRemoteDrillPlan` and
`verifyRemoteDrillPlan` from
`@expo/snapback-cli/deployment-control` before it exposes any provisioning action.
The resulting `snapback.remote-drill-plan.v1` artifact binds the registered
provider/account/region/origin and exact driver bytes to:

- compute and encrypted persistent-volume classes;
- distinct immutable artifact and separately permissioned backup stores;
- TLS issuer, automated renewal, supervisor, restart, and interruption rules;
- bounded redacted log sink and retention;
- external control, admission-key, state, and replay-floor handles; and
- a currency, estimate, maximum monthly cost, estimate-provenance digest, and
  the six included cost components.

The plan explicitly retains that the profile does not claim HA, autoscaling,
multi-region operation, zero downtime, untrusted multi-tenancy, or a managed
service SLA. It is owner-only, content-addressed, expires after one hour, and
contains an exact confirmation token. Verification rechecks the retained
content identity, current target/driver binding, confirmation, expiry,
infrastructure separation, cost ceiling, and nonclaims. There is intentionally
no provisioning apply path yet: constructing or verifying this plan records
choices but does not authorize spend or create resources.

## Retain a content-addressed deploy plan

Planning re-verifies the release, calls the adapter's read-only inspection, and
binds both observations into a 15-minute immutable plan:

```sh
snapback deploy plan .snapback/releases/<release-digest> \
  --target target-preview-1 \
  --reason "preview acceptance" \
  --json
```

The plan records exact identities, the observed activation generation and
active release, release and manifest digests, ordered lifecycle steps, every
blocking GAP, and an exact confirmation token. Repeating the same operation id,
reason, time, release, target, and provider facts produces the same plan id.

Apply consumes the exact retained plan and release:

```sh
snapback deploy apply <plan-id> \
  --target <id> \
  --release <release-dir> \
  --confirm <token>
```

It verifies the content identity, target, confirmation, expiry, GAP set, exact
release bytes, and fresh activation generation before any adapter mutation. At
this checkpoint every ordinary release remains activation-ineligible, so
normal apply fails with `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_PLAN_BLOCKED`.

Behind that fence, the common apply engine is implemented. It acquires a
provider lease and invokes digest-bound, idempotent adapter steps for immutable
upload, inactive provisioning, compatibility preflight, verified backup,
staging, activation, served-path verification, and lease release. Each step is
retained immediately in an owner-only journal and a hash-chained final receipt.
An interruption resumes the same `operationId`; an adapter failure invokes
rollback and lease release. A production call rejects a step without a verified
`remoteProviderAttestation` as `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_REMOTE_EVIDENCE_REQUIRED` and
rolls it back.

The deterministic lifecycle harness exercises this entire protocol, including
interruption/retry and failure/rollback, but every resulting receipt has
`remoteEvidence: false` plus a blocking GAP. It cannot satisfy the hosted
profile. No ordinary release verifier returns `activationEligible: true`, and
no remote provider driver or hosted receipt has been witnessed.

Retained control authority is read through a descriptor opened with
`O_NOFOLLOW`, not by trusting a pathname checked earlier. Owner-only artifacts
must remain single-link and unchanged across the bounded read. Qualification
and prepared-release inputs use the same descriptor-first, single-link rule.
Control writes fsync both the new bytes and containing directory before the
result is treated as retained authority.

## Qualify an adapter and prepare a release

Production planning has two additional, closed artifact gates. An adapter
qualification binds the exact target, complete profile, driver digest,
provider account, region, and origin to remote evidence for all of:

- identity fencing and immutable upload read-back;
- TLS/origin and hosted-auth behavior;
- public health/acceptance, logs, and authenticated inspection;
- compatibility plus code-only rollback;
- isolated backup/restore and interruption resume;
- secret/private-data scans; and
- the concrete cost and capacity boundary.

The `hostedAuth` claim cannot be satisfied by that label and a generic
attestation alone. The qualification embeds a content-addressed executed drill
receipt binding the exact target and browser artifact to all five positive
static support axes, a maximum-five-minute deployment admission, disabled
operator surface, excluded direct-bearer seam, compatible handler, and live
limiter/invalidation/serialized-authority health under the same admission
epoch. It requires zero GAPs and remote-provider evidence. The receipt proves
the qualification-time drill; serving activation still needs a fresh admission
and live health.

A prepared release then binds that qualification to one base release plus
runtime/server artifacts, signature, SBOM, provenance, compatibility
generations, migration/rollback envelope, health and acceptance probes, and
configuration requirements. Both artifacts are content-addressed, require a
closed evidence inventory, and must retain zero GAPs before they can produce an
eligible plan.

`@expo/snapback-cli` exports `createHostedAuthDrillReceipt`,
`createAdapterQualificationManifest`, and `createPreparedReleaseManifest` for
adapter implementations. The producers derive target, provider, account,
region, origin, driver, qualification, and base-release bindings instead of
accepting those identities from the caller. They also require every one of the
eleven qualification claims and ten prepared-release evidence classes exactly
once, then derive the content identities consumed by the verifier.

```sh
snapback deploy plan <release-dir> \
  --target <id> \
  --reason "qualified preview" \
  --adapter-qualification <qualification.json> \
  --prepared-release <prepared-release.json>
```

The verifier requires the exact
`trusted-single-tenant-app-complete.v1` profile in the target, base release,
qualification, and prepared release. The producers do not run provider
operations or manufacture remote attestations: their evidence inputs must come
from the concrete adapter's retained drill. There is still no codegen
capability manifest or concrete remote drill for that profile, so the producer
and verifier contracts do not make current releases eligible. A
caller-supplied boolean or an evidence-looking provider name cannot replace
the artifacts.

## Start a hosted handler through the authenticated gate

The native server has the target-neutral consumer for a real adapter's hosted
startup authority, and `@expo/snapback-cli/hosted-admission-producer` supplies the
provider-neutral producer contract. Before each handler boot,
`prepareHostedAdmissionBoot` awaits the adapter's atomic advancement of
`senderReplayEpochFloor` in a monotone store outside the application backup
set and verifies its content-addressed receipt. Only then does it create
previously unused exact-0600 admission and key projections. The 32-byte MAC key
comes from the target's provider secret manager and conforms to
`schemas/auth.hosted-admission-key.schema.json`; it is never an application
config value or release, backup, log, or receipt component.

The adapter starts the runtime with both strict owner-only files:

```sh
snapback start \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --db /var/lib/snapback/app.sqlite3 \
  --auth-deployment hosted \
  --hosted-admission /run/snapback/hosted-admission.json \
  --hosted-admission-key /run/secrets/snapback-hosted-admission-key.json
```

Before it opens the database or binds a listener, the runtime verifies the
closed envelope shape, key identity, canonical MAC, canonical HTTPS origin,
five-minute admission lifetime, exact finite throttle policy, and positive
hosted facts. It then reconciles the external replay floor into SQLite before
publishing hosted posture. Every 15 seconds it re-authenticates the envelope;
a live refresh may advance admission, limiter, and invalidation epochs, but
cannot change deployment, handler incarnation, or the boot's replay floor. A
bad or missing refresh never extends authority: new work fails closed when the
last authenticated admission expires.

`refreshHostedAdmissionProjection` authenticates the current envelope with the
provider key before replacing it atomically. It constructs the next admission
from the authenticated boot facts, so deployment, configuration, support,
throttle policy, handler incarnation, and replay floor cannot be substituted
by the refresher. Its non-secret external-floor, boot-projection, and refresh
receipts have Rust-owned closed schemas and explicitly retain
`remoteEvidence: false`.

This is the producer protocol, not the concrete provider implementation. No
provider currently supplies and remotely attests the rollback-external
counter, secret-manager retrieval, supervised refresh operation, or complete
drill, so hosted capability and gate 1 remain open.

## Inspect retained backups

A backup can be planned and applied independently of a deployment. The plan
binds a fresh target observation, active release, activation and schema
generations, requested retention policy, operation id, expiry, and exact
confirmation:

```sh
snapback backup create plan \
  --target target-preview-1 \
  --reason "scheduled recovery point" \
  --retention-policy thirty-days

snapback backup create apply <backup-plan-id> \
  --target target-preview-1 \
  --confirm <create-backup-token>
```

Apply rechecks the same generations, acquires the deployment lease, requires
the adapter to return a content-addressed manifest only after component
read-back, verifies that the adapter honored the planned retention policy, and
proves that backup creation did not change the active release or activation
generation. A successful deploy lifecycle also retains its pre-deploy backup
manifest independently of the deploy receipt:

```sh
snapback backup list --target target-preview-1 --json
snapback backup verify <backup-id> --target target-preview-1 --json
```

The manifest binds deployment, database, stream, pre-deploy release, schema,
encryption/storage/retention classes, component byte/object/hash facts, and
verification times. It must explicitly exclude `application-secrets` and
`control-plane-credentials`. `backup verify` rechecks the owner-only manifest
content identity and the adapter's component read-back attestations; it does
not refetch a remote object and therefore is not a substitute for the remote
restore drill.

## Verify the control audit chain

Every deploy, backup, code-only rollback, destructive restore, and restore
activation apply writes a mandatory `began` fact before its first provider
mutation and a terminal outcome afterward. Log/admin inspection, backup
list/verify, and restore verification also append bounded privileged-read
facts. The owner-only ledger rejects secret-shaped field classes and chains
each Rust-schema-owned event to its predecessor:

```sh
snapback audit verify --control-root <control-dir>
```

Use `--audit-actor <portable-id>` on control commands to name the local
operator explicitly. If omitted, the CLI records the portable local OS user
when available. A busy, corrupt, unsafe, or unwritable audit intake fails
closed before a privileged action proceeds. The local chain detects accidental
loss or modification; it is not described as tamper-proof because the same
operator controls the store.

## Plan and apply a code-only rollback

Rollback is a separate content-addressed mutation; it never rewinds data. Its
planner consumes the destination release, prepared-release manifest, and
adapter qualification, then uses authenticated live inspection to prove that
the destination can read the current schema generation and declares
`rollbackMode: codeOnly`:

```sh
snapback deploy rollback plan \
  --target <id> \
  --release <destination-release-dir> \
  --prepared-release <prepared-release.json> \
  --adapter-qualification <qualification.json> \
  --reason "return to prior compatible release"

snapback deploy rollback apply <rollback-plan-id> \
  --target <id> \
  --release <destination-release-dir> \
  --prepared-release <prepared-release.json> \
  --adapter-qualification <qualification.json> \
  --confirm <token>
```

Apply re-verifies every artifact and the live active release, activation
generation, and schema generation before acquiring a lease. It runs
compatibility preflight, switches to the destination under a new generation,
verifies the served path, and retains a hash-chained maintenance receipt.
`forwardFix`, `restoreRequired`, and `blocked` are not silently treated as
code-only rollback.

## Restore into an isolated destination, then activate explicitly

Restore consumes a retained verified backup and initially leaves the
destination inactive with external effects fenced:

```sh
snapback restore plan <backup-id> \
  --source-target <source-id> \
  --target <destination-id> \
  --reason "isolated recovery drill"

snapback restore apply <restore-plan-id> \
  --target <destination-id> \
  --confirm <destroy-and-restore-token>

snapback restore verify <paused-receipt-id> \
  --target <destination-id>
```

V1 refuses production destinations. An empty preview destination must be in an
isolated state. A nonempty destination additionally requires both its exact
active release and fresh application sentinel via `--replace-release` and
`--destination-sentinel`; neither fact is inferred from an alias.

Apply fences traffic and external workers, restores the backup into the
inactive destination, verifies component hashes and an application sentinel
with external effects disabled, and retains a `restoredPaused` receipt. That
receipt is not serving authority. Activation requires another fresh plan and
confirmation:

```sh
snapback restore activate plan <paused-receipt-id> \
  --target <destination-id> \
  --release <restored-release-dir> \
  --prepared-release <prepared-release.json> \
  --adapter-qualification <qualification.json> \
  --reason "activate verified recovery"

snapback restore activate apply <activation-plan-id> \
  --target <destination-id> \
  --release <restored-release-dir> \
  --prepared-release <prepared-release.json> \
  --adapter-qualification <qualification.json> \
  --confirm <activate-restore-token>
```

The activation plan rechecks the inactive state, restore generation, sentinel,
log sink, paused receipt, restored release bytes, prepared-release manifest,
and target-specific adapter qualification. Apply re-verifies them, acquires a
new lease, re-enables serving under a new activation generation, verifies the
public path, and retains a separate `restoreActivated` receipt.

## Query bounded logs and authenticated inspection

The adapter query protocol is separate from public health and ordinary target
identity inspection:

```sh
snapback logs --target <id> --since-ms <ms> --until-ms <ms> --limit 100
snapback inspect --target <id>
```

Responses are digest-bound to the request and exact target. Logs are limited to
500 structured entries per page and 32 bounded scalar payload fields per
entry. Credential-, request-body-, payment-, private-content-, query-argument-,
and result-shaped field names are rejected, as are known credential patterns.
An active target reporting dropped or backpressured logs fails log health.

Authenticated inspection returns only bounded digest facts for health,
dependencies, migration, backups, queues, connections, resources, generations,
capabilities, and recent control operations. Production commands require a
verified remote-provider attestation. The deterministic driver is accessible
only through the package test harness and remains `remoteEvidence: false`.

## Repair a refused build

- `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_SOURCE_UNVERSIONED`: initialize and commit the application
  repository so the release has an immutable source identity.
- `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_DIRTY_SOURCE`: commit the intended source, or use
  `--allow-dirty` only for a visibly dirty preview.
- `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_CAPABILITY_MISMATCH`: select a profile that supports every
  generated requirement; do not delete the requirement to make the build
  green.
- `SNAPBACK_RELEASE_FORBIDDEN_FILE`,
  `SNAPBACK_RELEASE_SECRET_SCAN_FAILED`, or
  `SNAPBACK_RELEASE_SOURCE_MAP_REFUSED`: remove the forbidden bytes from the
  release input and rotate any credential that entered a build tree.
- `SNAPBACK_RELEASE_ARTIFACT_TAMPERED`: discard the damaged retained directory
  and rebuild from reviewed source. Never patch a content-addressed closure in
  place.
- `SNAPBACK_ADAPTER_DRIVER_TAMPERED`: restore the reviewed adapter bytes or
  register a new never-reused target descriptor after reviewing the new digest.
- `SNAPBACK_TARGET_IDENTITY_MISMATCH`: stop and reconcile the descriptor with
  the provider account and origin; never override provider read-back.
- `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_PLAN_BLOCKED` or `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_PLAN_EXPIRED`: inspect the
  GAPs or create a fresh plan. A confirmation token does not waive either
  fence.
- `SNAPBACK_DEPLOY_REMOTE_EVIDENCE_REQUIRED`: the driver returned a local or
  unattested lifecycle result. The CLI rolls back; install a qualified remote
  adapter rather than relabeling the evidence.
- `SNAPBACK_MAINTENANCE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED`: use the exact token retained in
  the rollback, restore, or restore-activation plan; TTY presence is not
  confirmation.
- `SNAPBACK_RESTORE_STALE_PLAN` or
  `SNAPBACK_RESTORE_ACTIVATION_STALE_PLAN`: destination generation, release, or
  sentinel changed; discard the plan and inspect again.
- `SNAPBACK_ADAPTER_LOG_REDACTION_INVALID`: the adapter emitted a forbidden or
  unbounded log payload field. Fix the adapter schema/redactor; do not weaken
  the reader.
- `SNAPBACK_CONTROL_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE`: the mandatory append lane is locked or
  unwritable. Stop the privileged operation, preserve the store, and run
  `snapback audit verify`; do not bypass or delete audit history.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not call `deploy build` a deployment.** It grants no provider or traffic
  authority.
- **Do not suppress a blocking GAP.** Supply the named artifact or executed
  receipt through an accepted adapter contract.
- **Do not put secrets in a web bundle or generated directory.** Secret scans
  are a last refusal boundary, not a configuration mechanism.
- **Do not edit a retained release.** Its content address and read-back check
  are the authority.

---

# Deploying the Cloudflare proof

Snapback's Cloudflare target is real but narrow. The All Aboard Contract app
has been deployed and remotely proven over Workers, a coordinator Durable
Object with SQLite, a separate V8 action isolate, same-origin static/native
assets, WebSocket Hibernation, deploy-time secrets, and demand-armed alarms.
It is a proof profile—not a general hosted Snapback product.

The target profile id is `cloudflare-do-sqlite-v8`. Read the deployed
`GET /capability` or `/inspect` result before relying on a feature; its explicit
`capabilityGaps` outrank assumptions from the local guide.

## Prove the profile locally first

Use the Node major pinned in `.node-version` (24.x) and the repository-locked
Wrangler:

```sh fragment reason="Canonical local Cloudflare regression commands, composed with the repository Node pin."
volta run --node 24.18.0 -- node cloudflare/test/local-suite.mjs
volta run --node 24.18.0 -- node cloudflare/test/measure.mjs
```

The suite inventories every non-remote gate and currently runs 21 checks.
Miniflare validates protocol, storage, handlers, secrets, egress, cron, and
hibernation-event behavior, but it cannot prove platform eviction, placement,
or billing. Those require a real Cloudflare run.

## Understand the deployed shape

One gateway Worker routes HTTP, WebSockets, capability reads, and assets to one
named app coordinator Durable Object. That object's embedded SQLite owns:

- app and system tables;
- the per-app commit-version counter;
- change journal and storage-backed subscriptions;
- connection grants and cron/config state.

A mutation commits version, rows, and journal in one `transactionSync`. Live
fan-out happens directly from that commit—there is no polling tailer. App code
is compiled into the Worker at deploy time because deployed Workers forbid
dynamic evaluation; changing schema/handlers is a redeploy, not a bundle load.

Handlers run through the stripped, single-sourced V8 harness. Queries and
mutations receive only generated `ctx` powers. Actions run in a separate
handler Worker so a slow external fetch cannot queue the coordinator's
transactional work.

## Deploy All Aboard

Deployment mutates a real Cloudflare account. Use a Workers + Durable
Objects-scoped token and an independently generated admin token; never commit
either:

```sh fragment reason="All Aboard selection added to the canonical cloudflare/README.md deployment sequence."
bun install --frozen-lockfile
export CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=...
export CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=...
export SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN=...
SNAPBACK_CF_APP=all-aboard ./cloudflare/deploy.sh
```

The script builds the same-origin Contract/native bundle, verifies the
repo-local Wrangler and locks, deploys handler dependencies before the gateway,
attests the exact active Worker version, and performs the final gateway deploy
after secret changes. On a partial failure it attempts to restore previously
active Worker versions; ambiguous account/API state fails closed.

An absent local `SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN` is not evidence that the remote secret
is absent. Deployment reports absent, present-and-preserved, or unknown; only
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN_REMOVE=1` requests attested removal.

## Configure declared secret pools

All Aboard declares `caltrainFeed` and `directions`. Send one JSON object of
non-empty string arrays over stdin, never in argv or shell history:

```sh source=cloudflare/README.md
SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN=... node cloudflare/config-set.mjs \
  --url https://snapback-all-aboard-proof.<subdomain>.workers.dev \
  --entries-stdin < /secure/path/to/secret-pools.json
```

`config-set.mjs` reads the current generation, writes changed bindings plus a
new `SNAPBACK_CONFIG_GENERATION` in one `wrangler secret bulk` activation, then
polls authenticated `/config/status` until that generation and member counts
are attested as applied. It refuses value-bearing argv flags. Status returns
names, set/missing state, counts, and grant relationships—never values.

App actions receive descriptor handles only. Values unwrap at the coordinator's
host-fetch boundary into declared query-parameter or header slots:

```js source=cloudflare/app/all-aboard.app.js
  const response = await ctx.fetch({
    url,
    headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
    timeoutMs: 15_000,
    secretSlots: [{ placement: 'query-param', name: 'api_key', handle }],
  });
```

Ambient `fetch`, `.expose()`, and `.asBearer()` stay unavailable in the app
isolate. The host validates HTTP(S), descriptor ownership and placement,
enforces action/fetch deadlines and bounded response bodies, and redacts secret
values before any response or diagnostic re-enters app code. This is not a
general egress claim: the two All Aboard placement shapes are proven, but a
destination allowlist is still a declared gap.

## Run the remote proof

After secrets are applied, run the real-deployment acceptance:

```sh fragment reason="All Aboard remote acceptance invocation from the runner header."
SNAPBACK_PROOF_URL=https://snapback-all-aboard-proof.<subdomain>.workers.dev \
SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN=... \
  node cloudflare/test/acceptance.remote.all-aboard.mjs
```

It proves cold start, same-origin Contract/native assets, ensure/seed, config
attestation, finite queries and mutations, real hibernating WebSocket push,
live 511/directions actions, demand-armed warm polling, eviction recovery, and
secret redaction. Expect minutes rather than seconds because it waits for a
real scheduled cycle.

For the notes proof, `cloudflare/test/acceptance.remote.mjs` additionally
records connected-idle billing windows and platform-eviction evidence. Cloudflare
analytics may settle several minutes later; re-read the emitted window before
calling observed-zero usage final.

## Hibernation, reconnect, and idle-to-zero

Server-held sockets use the Durable Object WebSocket Hibernation API. Durable
subscription rows, not isolate memory or socket attachments, are the recovery
authority. After wake/eviction, the object rehydrates them; socket loss takes a
fresh snapshot-with-subscribe. Retained-version resume and HTTP outbox delta
polling are explicit gaps.

The hosted kit socket's in-band durable surface is independently governed:
`live.kit-socket-request.schema.json` covers `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, and
`ping`; `live.kit-socket-reply.schema.json` covers the actually served
`pong`, `snapshot`, `current_as_of`, and `error` frames. Unsubscribe is
deliberately silent. The Cloudflare wire-schema gate validates real reply bytes
against that Rust-derived contract; the older proof socket's `type`-tagged
frames are a separate pinned protocol.

The coordinator uses no always-awake interval. All Aboard's `warmPoll` is a
single Durable Object alarm dispatcher job:

- first live demand arms the alarm;
- the last unsubscribe cancels it;
- `(jobName, scheduledAt)` durable claims make alarm retry idempotent;
- an app with no subscribers schedules zero warm-poll wakeups.

Real settled evidence includes a two-hour no-demand interval with observed-zero
request/execution estimates and hibernating connected-idle measurements. This
supports the narrow proof's idle-to-zero claim; it is not a scale or price
guarantee for arbitrary apps.

## Exact supported subset and non-claims

The manifest currently claims V8, Durable Object SQLite, serialized mutation
commits, syncable/online single-table queries, replace-only live subscriptions,
the witnessed outbound-action shapes, and demand-armed cron. Enforced limits
include row/storage size, wall-clock/CPU, and subscription counts.

It explicitly does **not** claim:

- hosted authentication (only `authMode: dev` is supported);
- offline retention/replay or optimistic replay;
- ephemeral realtime rooms;
- generalized outbound actions or an egress destination allowlist;
- calendar/Cron Trigger schedules;
- R2 asset upload, notifications, Postgres, code hot-load, untrusted hosted
  tenant code, multiple apps per deployment, or a hosted marketplace;
- local pages whose `targets:` omit `cloudflare`.

See [auth target honesty](../auth/targets.md) before exposing this deployment
to users. The local bearer/dev identity posture is not production hosted auth.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not call the proof a general Cloudflare target.** Inspect its manifest
  and keep every gap visible.
- **Do not deploy with an unlocked/ad-hoc Wrangler or `npx`.**
- **Do not pass secrets in argv, config files, logs, or app-visible errors.**
- **Do not add interval polling to keep the object warm.** Use hibernation and
  the one demand-armed alarm dispatcher.
- **Do not infer a successful local suite proves billing or eviction.** Run the
  remote evidence lane.

# Your first backend

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A Snapback backend is a directory — conventionally `<app>/snapback/` —
holding a handful of source-authored `.mjs` files plus a generated review
manifest and an ignored, regenerable artifact materialization:

For the current source/packed React path, start with
`snapback new my-app --template react`, install the generated dependencies,
and run `bun run dev`. That one script owns both this backend loop and Vite;
the exact public-versus-staged package boundary and seed-on-new-database
behavior are in [the authoring loop](./the-authoring-loop.md).

```text
myapp/
  snapback/
    schema.mjs        # source-authored schema (the source of truth)
    functions.mjs     # query/mutation/action definitions, JS handlers inline
    seed.json         # deterministic declarative seed
    generated/
      artifacts.json  # committed deterministic review manifest
      ...             # ignored cache materialization; never hand-edited
  .snapback/
    codegen-cache/    # complete graphs keyed by the complete inputsHash
```

You write the first three. Codegen owns everything under `generated/` and
`.snapback/codegen-cache/`. Commit `generated/artifacts.json` and only
consumer projections explicitly required by policy; see
[generated artifact custody](./generated-artifacts.md). (Apps on the
[legacy bundled-module form](#legacy-compatibility-bundled-handler-modules)
author one more file, `handlers.mjs`.)

## Declare the schema

All authoring helpers come from `packages/snapback-codegen/define.mjs`
(demos import it via the `demos/_kit/define.mjs` shim). A schema is tables
of validated fields, with chainable `.index(...)` and `.sync()`:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/schema.mjs
import { defineSchema, defineTable, v } from '../../_kit/define.mjs';

export default defineSchema({
  todos: defineTable({
    title: v.string(),
    completed: v.boolean(),
    userId: v.string(),
  })
    // by_user backs the user-scoped live query's index-first lookup.
    .index('by_user', ['userId'])
    // Declared syncable so it can back the restricted syncable-live subset.
    .sync(),
});
```

The complete validator set: `v.string()`, `v.principal()`, `v.id(table)`,
`v.boolean()`, `v.integer()`, `v.real()` / `v.number()`, `v.json()`,
`v.object({...})`, and `v.optional(inner)`. `defineSchema` also takes an
options object:
`ephemeral:` (a `defineEphemeral(...)` — see the
[presence recipe](../recipes/presence-cursors.md) and complete
[ephemeral-state reference](../realtime/ephemeral-state.md)), `auth:`
(`{ mode: 'dev' | 'sessions' }` — see
[auth/sessions-and-principals](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md)), and
`requiredCapabilities:`.

The system fields `_id`, `_version`, `_createdAt`, `_updatedAt` are
server-owned. Declaring one is a hard error
(`SNAPBACK_SCHEMA_SYSTEM_FIELD`), and handlers never set timestamps.

## Define functions

There are two authoring styles, freely mixed in one `functions.mjs`:

1. **Declarative plans** (`defineQuery`, `defineLiveQuery`,
   `defineMutation`) — built from expression helpers, deterministic, no JS
   runtime involved.
2. **Inline JS handlers** (`defineJsQuery`, `defineJsLiveQuery`,
   `defineJsMutation`, `defineAction`) — one direct, self-contained
   `handler:` expression colocated with its arguments, result contract, and
   declared reads/writes, run against the injected `ctx`.

A declarative query — filter, order, index, and the server-derived user id:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const listTodosOnce = defineQuery({
  table: 'todos',
  args: {},
  filter: [eq('userId', authUserId())],
  order: [asc('_createdAt')],
  index: 'by_user',
});
```

A JS mutation and a JS live query in the paved inline form — each definition
carries its `handler` directly, next to `args`, `result`, and the declared
`reads`/`writes`:

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/inline-result-contracts.test.mjs
  export const createTodo = defineJsMutation({
    args: { title: v.string() },
    writes: ['todos'],
    result: results.value(v.id('todos')),
    handler: async (ctx, args) => ctx.db.insert('todos', { title: args.title }),
  });
  export const watchTodos = defineJsLiveQuery({
    args: {},
    reads: ['todos'],
    result: results.documents('todos'),
    handler: async (ctx) => ctx.db.query('todos').collect(),
  });
```

(That excerpt is transcluded from the codegen package's inline-handler
conformance test over a minimal `todos` table, so this page breaks if the
paved form drifts. Fuller inline examples — index-first lookups, auth
scoping, multi-table writes — are transcluded from
`demos/signal-desk/snapback/functions.mjs` on the reference pages linked
below.)

A declarative mutation, for comparison:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const editTitle = defineMutation({
  args: { id: v.string(), title: v.string() },
  plan: patch('todos', arg('id'), { title: arg('title') }),
  returns: returnChangedCount(),
});
```

Use a declarative plan when the plan vocabulary expresses the operation; use
an inline JS handler for bounded logic it cannot express.
`demos/todo-v2/snapback/functions.mjs` is a fully declarative app, and
`demos/signal-desk/snapback/functions.mjs` mixes declarative live queries
with inline JS mutations — the side-by-sides worth reading when choosing.
The reference pages carry the complete semantics:
[queries](../backend/queries.md), [mutations](../backend/mutations.md), and
[actions](../backend/actions-and-fetch.md).

## Inside a JS handler

A handler receives only the injected `ctx` and its validated `args` — no
imports, no `process`/env, no timers, no network, no direct storage. The
core `ctx.db` surface: `ctx.db.query(table).withIndex(name).eq(field, value)`
`.in(field, [...])`.`order(field, dir)`.`collect()`, plus
`ctx.db.get(table, id)`, `ctx.db.insert(table, values)`,
`ctx.db.patch(table, id, values)`, `ctx.db.delete(table, id)`, and
`ctx.auth.userId` — the server-derived identity
([never client-asserted](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md)).

Inline v1 is deliberately self-contained: it does not capture imports,
sibling helpers, or outer constants, so put all application logic and locals
inside the direct handler expression. Class syntax, dynamic import, `eval`,
and `Function` are refused during generation.
[Queries](../backend/queries.md) covers the capture limits; the governing
spec is
[LLP 0108](repo:llp/0108-inline-handlers-and-result-contracts.spec.md).

Declare what a handler returns. JS query and live-query handlers return an
**array of rows** (`[]` for missing, `[row]` for present) described by
`results.documents(table)` or `results.records(v.object({...}))`; mutations
and actions use `results.value(validator)` or `results.document(table)`.
Omitting `result` is an explicit degraded `unknown` contract. The complete
result-contract vocabulary and runtime-validation rules are on
[queries](../backend/queries.md) and [mutations](../backend/mutations.md).

Membership declarations additionally generate query-side
`ctx.permissions.<declaration>` checks and mutation-only
`ctx.membership.<declaration>` operations. See
[scoped roles and memberships](../auth/scoped-roles.md) for their typed surface
and transition rules.

## Seed deterministically

```json source=demos/todo/snapback/seed.json
{
  "tables": {
    "todos": [
      { "_id": "seed_todo_1", "title": "Read the Snapback explainer", "completed": true, "userId": "user_ada" },
      { "_id": "seed_todo_2", "title": "Build the todo demo", "completed": false, "userId": "user_ada" },
      { "_id": "seed_todo_3", "title": "Write the diary", "completed": false, "userId": "user_ada" },
      { "_id": "seed_todo_4", "title": "Plan the kanban demo", "completed": false, "userId": "user_grace" }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Generate and load

```sh
node packages/snapback-codegen/index.mjs myapp/snapback
```

Codegen **fails closed**: on any error it leaves the previously serveable
graph intact and exits 1 with stable diagnostic codes
(`QUERY_UNKNOWN_FIELD`, `FUNCTION_RESERVED_EXPORT`, ...). On success it writes
a complete input-hash cache and materializes `myapp/snapback/generated/` for
compatibility — server manifests
(`schema.manifest.json`, `functions.manifest.json`), the client binding
surface (`api.mjs` + `api.d.ts`), Contract binding modules under
`contract/`, per-function argument schemas under `operations/`, and
`artifacts.json` carrying digests, custody, the `inputsHash`, and the
deterministic author summary. Commit the review manifest, not the ordinary
cache projections.

A running server loads the app over its admin API — the kit client wraps
the endpoints:

```js source=demos/todo/surfaces/headless/run.mjs
  await db.loadSchema(gen('schema.manifest.json'));
  await db.loadFunctions(gen('functions.manifest.json'));
  await db.reset();
  await db.seed(JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(backendDir, 'seed.json'), 'utf8')));
```

For a `dev`-mode app,
`db.ensureApp({ schema, functions, seed })` is the idempotent form: it
provisions only what's missing and seeds only empty tables.

Sessions-mode provisioning is deliberately explicit and admin-authorized:

```js fragment reason="generated manifests and seed come from the app build"
const db = new SnapbackClient(baseUrl, { adminToken });
await db.ensureApp({
  intent: 'provision',
  requestedMode: 'sessions',
  schema,
  functions,
  seed,
  routes,
});
```

The untagged legacy body is refused once sessions mode is active. Explicit
provisioning always carries the client's configured admin token and remains
non-production-profile gated, even when artifact hashes already match. A fresh
`dev → sessions` provision stages the sessions deployment and closes app data
until the required process restart consumes it; same-mode sessions provisioning
is idempotent without weakening the gate. Explicit mode provisioning does not
reinterpret route identity: it validates `routes` against the same candidate
schema/functions pair and installs them only with that deployment.

Then call it. Function references are the generated `api.<name>` objects
from `generated/api.mjs`, and mutations return structured results:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const created = await db.mutate(api.createTodo, { args: { title: 'Buy milk' }, userId: ADA });
```

Continue with [the authoring loop](./the-authoring-loop.md) for the full
edit-regenerate-test cycle, and
[testing/acceptance](../testing/acceptance.md) for the harness.

## Legacy compatibility: bundled handler modules

Before inline handlers landed, the JS style split every definition from its
logic: the definition names a bundled module and export
(`source` / `exportName`), and the logic registers on a global in a separate
authored `handlers.mjs` next to `functions.mjs`. This form remains fully
supported — `demos/todo` still uses it — but it is the compatibility lane,
not the paved path for new work.

The definition names its handler and declares its writes:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const createTodo = defineJsMutation({
  args: { title: v.string() },
  source: 'handlers.mjs',
  exportName: 'createTodo',
  writes: ['todos'],
});
```

The bundled module registers its logic on a global and receives the same
injected `ctx` and bounded `ctx.db` surface as an inline handler:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/handlers.mjs
globalThis.__snapbackHandlers = {
  async listTodos(ctx) {
    return await ctx.db
      .query('todos')
      .withIndex('by_user')
      .eq('userId', ctx.auth.userId)
      .order('_createdAt', 'asc')
      .collect();
  },

  async createTodo(ctx, args) {
    const title = String(args.title ?? '').trim();
    if (!title) throw new Error('todo title is required');
    return await ctx.db.insert('todos', {
      title,
      completed: false,
      userId: ctx.auth.userId,
    });
  },
```

The `{ source, exportName }` lane remains useful for existing apps already
on the split and for logic that genuinely needs imported or sibling helpers,
which inline v1 deliberately refuses to capture. One definition declares
`handler` or `source`/`exportName`, never both — mixed or missing
discriminants fail generation with
`SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_HANDLER_FORM_INVALID`.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not hand-wire HTTP glue for app data.** The generated `api.mjs`
  references plus the kit client (or the Contract adapter /
  React arm) are the product path; raw `fetch` against `/query/...` is how
  demos accumulated unauditable glue before the kit existed.
- **Do not start new JS functions on the bundled `handlers.mjs` split.**
  Inline `handler:` is the paved form; the `source`/`exportName` module lane
  is compatibility for existing apps and for logic that needs sibling
  modules.
- **Do not edit anything under `generated/` or `.snapback/codegen-cache/`.**
  Regenerate. The server
  rejects stale artifacts loudly (`SNAPBACK_STALE_SCHEMA_ARTIFACT_VERSION`,
  `SNAPBACK_STALE_CONTRACT_DATA_INPUTS_HASH`).
- **Do not set `_createdAt`/`_updatedAt`/`_id`/`_version`.** Server-owned;
  declaring them in a schema is a hard error.
- **Do not assert identity from the client.** `ctx.auth.userId` is derived
  server-side; see [auth](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md).
